sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 'Unpublished Field Materials: Languages: Jukunoid' (JkOP.htm) and 'Endangered Jukunoid languages' (ELJkdOP.htm), rogerblench.info; Common Crawl 2024-02 and the Internet Archive 2008/2015/2025 captures; whole-site the Internet Archive's index listings
sources.note: Pages list only Jibu dictionary, Kuteb grammar (Koops) and Kuteb photos. the only 'Bete' paths are Côte d'Ivoire Bété artefact photos.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid bete1261 and reference 302077 (Prischnegg 2008); Glottolog JSON classification

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2026. Rethinking the classification of 'South Jukunoid'. Paper, Third Conference on Bantoid Languages and Linguistics (Bantoid 3), University at Buffalo, May 20-21, 2026
sources.note: Comparative paper; newest treatment of the group; may cite or reproduce whatever Bete data exist (Koops?) and name the current custodians of Bete materials.

sources.citation: Endangered Languages Project (ELCat), 'Bete' (ELP id 4018), Internet Archive copy 2025-01-19
sources.note: Sources listed: Dimmendaal & Voeltz 2007 (Routledge encyclopedia ch. 7), World Oral Literature Project, LL-MAP 2012, Ethnologue 16. Vitality data only; no linguistic description, no Koops manuscript listed.

sources.citation: Kempf, Viktoria & Tamara Prischnegg. 2020. A sketch of Akum (Southern Jukunoid). Afrika und Übersee 93: 287-326. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.215
sources.note: Sister language only. Names Bete once, as a member of 'the whole Southern Jukunoid language group (Bezen, Bete, Lufu, Akum, Kuteb, Yukuben, Kapya)' (p. 296-297). Akum has a three-tone system (sec. 2.3); no word on stress, and nothing on Bete phonology.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2019 [PDF dated 2020]. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, edition IV. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (draft PDF from author's site; Internet Archive copy 2025-05-23, 198 pp.)
sources.note: Entry 46 'Bete': '3. Taraba State, Wukari LGA, Bete town. 4. Language dying out.' — no sources, references or linguistic data; classification list (p. 98) places Bete under Jukunoid: Yukuben-Kutep. Bibliography item 'Briggs, Kathleen 1972. An introductory description of the Bete language. University of Ibadan MA thesis' is cited under entry 47 Bete-Bendi (Obudu; = bete1262), not this language. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Pozdniakov, Konstantin. 2018. The numeral system of Proto-Niger-Congo: A step-by-step reconstruction (Niger-Congo Comparative Studies 2). Berlin: Language Science Press. Table 4.34 'Jukunoid numerals' (col. 1 Bete (Juk.)) and Appendix E, Table E.25 (source: Tamara Prischnegg via Chan).
sources.note: Only untoned simplified numeral forms for Bete (fife?, ha, ta, pé, 5, 5+1.. 10 wo) in a comparative table; no phonological commentary on Bete. Second-hand from Prischnegg/Chan.

sources.citation: Chan, Eugene S. L. (ed.). Numeral Systems of the World's Languages: 'Bete, Taraba state, Nigeria'. Data provided by Dr. Tamara Prischnegg, Institut für Afrikawissenschaften, Universität Wien, 15 April 2013. Leipzig: MPI-EVA (web page).
sources.note: Tone-marked numerals only (1 uʃɪ́ʃe, 2 máhá, 3 batà, 4 beɲè, 5 vatsòŋ, 6 vatsòŋ uʃí, 7 vatsòŋ máhá, 8 vatsòŋ batà, 9 vatsòŋ eɲè, 10 uwo, 11 ulotí) with acute/grave marks implying at least a H/L lexical tone contrast; the only comment is 'Bete number system is based on five..'. Wordlist-only data, no statement on tone inventory or stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. [2012]. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, edition III (draft PDF; Internet Archive copy 2013-04-20, 125 pp.)
sources.note: Entry 45 'Bete': Taraba State, Wukari LGA, Bete town; language dying out; unclassified. No sources. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: UNESCO, Communication and Information Sector. c. 2005. 'Bete' - language profile, Atlas on endangered languages (UNESCO-CI portal topic ID 9910). Web page, the Internet Archive captures 2011-2016.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing linguistic: vitality and ethnographic notes only ('The language remains unclassified regarding its linguistic affiliation. It is probably related to the Lufu and Bibi languages.'; six sub-groups Aphan (Afan), Ruke, Osu, Agu, Botsu, Humiyan). Useful only for identity (Bibi treated as a separate related lect) when weighing Koops 2004 'born at Bibi'.

sources.citation: Brenzinger, Matthias (ed.). 1992. Language Death: Factual and Theoretical Explorations with Special Reference to East Africa. (Contributions to the Sociology of Language 64.) Berlin; New York: Mouton de Gruyter. ISBN 3-11-013404-7. [copies we hold = the whole 456-page volume; target-language coverage is in Sommer, Gabriele, 'A survey on language death in Africa', pp. 301-417 (doi:10.1515/9783110870602.301), with minor mentions in Batibo, 'The fate of ethnic languages in Tanzania', pp. 85-98, and Legère, 'Language shift in Tanzania', pp. 99-115]
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Sociolinguistic questionnaire entry only (names, classification, status, speaker numbers, location, references); nothing on stress, accent or tone.

sources.note: Stubs; cite only Ethnologue, Crozier & Blench 1992, UNESCO profile, Blench 2019 Atlas and Blench 2026 Bantoid-3 paper (academia.edu, 403). No phonology.
